old: Three candidates were considered for what the caveat is, and two were ruled out on the arithmetic. (1) That the block is a diversity purchase: refuted by the shape of the product. A /24 is one contiguous prefix, so it is one announcing AS, one registration class and one lease, which is a single rung-3 unit and the opposite of independent exits; 256 addresses behind one prefix do not survive the failure that matters, a prefix-level block or withdrawal. (2) That the per-address price is a reason to prefer the block: confirmed as arithmetic and rejected as a conclusion. USD 1.95 x 256 = USD 499.20 against USD 2.80 x 256 = USD 716.80 over 30 days, so the block is about 30 percent cheaper per address, but it buys concentration rather than independence. (3) That the registration class and announcing AS could be checked: refuted, because no test IP is published for the block product, and the sibling single-IP page is a different product whose address would not prove the block's. That third one is the caveat in the verdict. One sample underlies every number: two vendor pages read once, on 2026-10-24, with no invoice, no trial and no probe behind them. What would settle it is a trial or a purchased block, one address checked against RIPE or ARIN whois for the registration class and a looking glass for the announcing AS. The identity tier has no URL of its own: the signup fields (email, password, verification code; no phone, no ID) come from the capture and the capture names no signup page, so no evidence row carries it. The interface token is `unknown` rather than a protocol name because the capture states delivery and shaping but never the access protocol; the schema's interface vocabulary has no SOCKS5 or HTTP-proxy member, so a protocol guess would have been both an invention and a schema defect. No record in another topic is corrected here: this is the first LinkStatic record in the corpus.
